title: Is a Post-American World Inevitable?
gist: In a moderated conversation, Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi debate Mark Leonard over whether U.S. alliances can be reforged after Trump (their view) or whether the U.S.-led order has permanently ended (Leonard's view), surfacing sharper specifics than their companion essays: contested export-shift statistics, a live warning that the global economy is 'teetering' if the Iran conflict continues, Campbell's correction that Xi Jinping's 'great changes unseen in a century' points to Chinese-led order rather than disorder, and Leonard's case that some 'managed proliferation' (European and Asian allies building their own deterrents) may be a stabilizing rather than dangerous outcome.

themes.theme: A live economic warning: the Iran conflict risks tipping into global recession

insights.claim: Kurt Campbell warns the global economy is 'teetering right now' because of the continuing Gulf conflict; the U.S. has so far absorbed disruptions to fertilizer, petrochemicals, sulfur, and helium supplies only because of reserves built up over time, and if the conflict continues, shortages will start to bite the global economy in ways that could trigger a genuinely difficult global recession.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A direct, named warning from a former senior U.S. official that continued Gulf conflict could tip the global economy into recession once existing strategic reserves of fertilizer, petrochemicals, sulfur, and helium are exhausted — a concrete catalyst and set of commodities to monitor for supply-chain stress signals.
insights.quote: We’ve been able, because of larger reserves that have built up over time, of fertilizer and petrochemicals and sulfur and a variety of other things like helium, that will be able to continue with these disruptions. That is not the case... a global recession at this juncture would just complicate all of our endeavors going forward.
insights.locator: closing exchange on what could change the outcome

insights.claim: In live conversation, Rush Doshi cited European exports to China as having fallen by roughly 30 percent over the relevant period while exports to the United States rose by roughly 15 percent — figures that diverge from the more precise breakdown in his companion written essay (which cited a 15 percent fall to China and a 30 percent rise to the U.S.), illustrating how even the authors' own cited statistics shift somewhat between formats.
insights.speaker: Rush Doshi
insights.so_what: Flags a data inconsistency between the podcast and the companion essay on the same underlying trend (European export reorientation away from China and toward the U.S.), a reminder to treat precise percentage figures cited in live discussion with some caution relative to the sourced written piece.
insights.quote: look at the trade statistics. The biggest trend in the last five years is that European exports to China have fallen by like 30%. They’ve gone up to the United States by 15%. And the same is true of Korea and of India as well.
insights.locator: Doshi's response on hedging and trade trends

insights.claim: Rush Doshi notes the share of European defense spending going to American companies was around 50 percent from 2022 to 2024 post-Ukraine, and argues that even if that share fell to 40 or 35 percent, it would represent sensible resilience-building rather than a catastrophic decoupling from the United States.
insights.speaker: Rush Doshi
insights.so_what: Offers an explicit reframing of European defense-spending 'de-risking' as a benign, even healthy adjustment rather than alliance erosion — a useful lens for interpreting future declines in the U.S. share of European defense procurement.
insights.quote: the American companies, with European defense spending. Until recently, that share was like 50%. From 2022 to 2024, post-Ukraine, half of all European spending went to American companies on defense. Let’s say that number goes down from 50% to 40% or 35%. Is that a catastrophic decoupling or de-risking from the U.S.? Or is that sensible resilience?
insights.locator: Doshi's response on hedging and trade trends

insights.claim: Germany plans to spend 500 billion euros on defense over the coming period, and by 2029 will be spending as much on defense as France and the United Kingdom combined.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified forecast of German defense spending (500 billion euros, exceeding France+UK combined by 2029) directly relevant to European defense-sector investment and to assessing the shifting center of gravity within European military capability.
insights.quote: Germany’s going to spend 500 billion euros on this over the next period of time. Once you start doing that over a long period of time. Germany will be spending as much as France and the UK combined by 2029.

themes.theme: Concrete national examples of allied hedging

insights.claim: Denmark, which previously had no substantial indigenous military and instead built 'spare parts' for U.S.-led expeditionary missions, is now rethinking its entire defense posture from the ground up toward territorial defense, driven by Trump's threats against Greenland.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A concrete national case study of an ally undertaking a fundamental doctrinal shift (from expeditionary plug-in force to territorial defense) in direct response to a specific U.S. threat — illustrates how Trump-era friction is producing durable structural changes in individual allied militaries, not just rhetoric.
insights.quote: if you take Denmark for example, which is maybe one of the most extreme countries, they didn’t really have a kind of indigenous military... And they’re now having to kind of rethink their entire position from the ground up. They’re going to be much more focused on territorial defense

insights.claim: A former Japanese national security adviser told Mark Leonard, on the record, 'I'm not sure if the U.S. will be there for us if we have a kind of problem' — a statement Leonard calls extraordinary for a Japanese diplomat to make publicly.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A striking, named-source anecdote of a senior Japanese security official publicly voicing doubt about U.S. reliability — a notable erosion-of-confidence data point for Indo-Pacific alliance credibility, especially given Japan's historically discreet public diplomacy.
insights.quote: I heard a former Japanese national security adviser say, “I’m not sure if the U.S. will be there for us if we have a kind of problem.” Which is a pretty extraordinary situation, for a Japanese diplomat to be saying things like that on the record in public.
insights.locator: Leonard's response on the case against pessimism

themes.theme: Clarifying what Xi Jinping's 'great changes' actually means

insights.claim: Kurt Campbell pushes back on Mark Leonard's framing that Xi Jinping's phrase 'great changes unseen in a century' refers to coming global disorder; Campbell argues Xi is instead describing his belief in a rising East and declining West — a distinctly China-led order, not chaos, which is 'the last thing' China wants to see on the global stage.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A meaningful analytical correction: China's own strategic vision is for a new, China-centered order rather than the 'un-order' Leonard describes — an important distinction for interpreting Chinese foreign-policy intent versus simply assuming Beijing is comfortable with global chaos.
insights.quote: When he says, "Changes unseen in a century," 100 years, he’s not talking about a coming disorder, Mark. He’s talking very clearly about his belief of a rising East and a declining West. He sees a different kind of order, that it’s China-led. He is not prescribing or believing that the coming period is going to be marked by disorder. That’s the last thing that China wants to see on the global stage.

insights.claim: Campbell argues China has doubled down on relationships with Russia and North Korea specifically, which creates deep anxieties in Europe and elsewhere, and that China's promised manufacturing engagement in Africa has been largely unfulfilled, mirroring the pattern of prior British, American, and other great powers' engagement there.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: Directly counters the narrative of China as a uniquely adept, unifying Global South partner by pointing to unfulfilled manufacturing promises in Africa and destabilizing deepened ties with Russia and North Korea.
insights.quote: where President Xi has really doubled down is on his relationships with countries like Russia and North Korea. And that is unambiguous, and it creates deep anxieties not just in Europe but elsewhere... The China promise of manufacturing and engagement in places like Africa has been largely unfulfilled

insights.claim: Mark Leonard describes Xi Jinping's 'holistic national security' concept as effectively the securitization of everything, citing China's extraordinary progress in a short period toward self-sufficiency in energy, high-end chips and computer products, and food security as evidence of successful preparation for a more weaponized global economy.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Frames China's domestic resilience-building (energy, chips, food self-sufficiency) as a deliberate, successful hedge against exactly the chokepoint-weaponization dynamics described in Leonard's companion essay — relevant to assessing China's relative resilience in any prolonged economic confrontation with the West.
insights.quote: Xi Jinping has this wholistic approach to national security, which basically means the securitization of everything. And if you look at the kind of vast amount of energy that’s gone into making China more self-sufficient and resilient on energy when it comes to chips and high-end computer products, when it comes to food security, it is extraordinarily impressive
insights.locator: Leonard's response on China's strategic positioning

insights.claim: Leonard argues China has been more successful positioning itself for a world without order than for handling the U.S. bilaterally, having pivoted from Cold War-style alliance-building rhetoric toward casting itself as a defender of sovereignty, and doubling down on relationships with Global South countries the Biden administration had converged around the G7 instead.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Suggests China's comparative advantage lies not in winning a bilateral standoff with Washington but in being structurally better positioned for a chaotic, non-aligned multipolar world — relevant to assessing where Chinese soft power gains are most durable (Global South) versus fragile (Europe, per Leonard's other comments on China's poor handling of Europe).
insights.quote: what I think is much more interesting... is more trying to position themselves as friends of sovereignty and status-seeking by countries who felt excluded or not necessarily well-represented in the old Western-based system.
insights.locator: Leonard's response on China's strategic positioning

themes.theme: Reframing proliferation and regional autonomy as potentially stabilizing

insights.claim: Mark Leonard argues that some forms of what looks like 'managed proliferation' — such as Germany and Poland working with France and the UK to build a deterrent capacity against Russia, or Japan and South Korea relying less on the United States — might not be catastrophic and could instead represent healthy resilience-building, contrary to the traditional view that more nuclear-armed or militarily autonomous states makes the world less safe.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A genuinely contrarian reframe worth flagging: rather than treating rising allied military autonomy or limited proliferation as pure alliance failure, Leonard suggests it could be a stabilizing adaptation — relevant to how investors and policymakers interpret European/Asian defense buildups.
insights.quote: one very good area of that is proliferation, for example, where there’s been a sort of norm against proliferation. Before, we thought that a world with more nuclear weapons would be a less safe one. But actually, having some sort of managed proliferation... is not a kind of terrible thing.

insights.claim: Leonard cites new diplomatic relations emerging between Saudi Arabia and Iran, developed as the United States withdrew from its traditional dominant regional role, as a genuinely positive outcome — noting that Jake Sullivan was heavily criticized for an essay published just days before October 7, 2025 arguing the Middle East was becoming more orderly, but that Saudi-Iranian channels have actually helped prevent even worse outcomes since.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Points to an under-appreciated positive development (durable Saudi-Iran channels) emerging directly from reduced U.S. regional dominance — a specific counter-example to the assumption that U.S. withdrawal automatically produces worse regional outcomes, and a pointed historical callback to Sullivan's since-criticized 'more orderly Middle East' essay.
insights.quote: one of the very positive things that’s happened in recent times as the U.S. has withdrawn from playing the role that it did earlier, was to see new diplomatic relations emerge between the Saudis and the Iranians... I know Jake Sullivan got in a lot of trouble for writing an essay for you, Dan, just a few days before the 7th of October, where he was talking about how the Middle East was becoming more orderly.

themes.theme: The real risk: domestic political feedback loops

insights.claim: Leonard identifies the single most dangerous dynamic as a negative feedback loop between a more chaotic and dangerous international order and the rise of ethno-nationalist parties to power in major countries, noting far-right parties currently lead opinion polls in most large European countries.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Names a specific compounding risk mechanism (international disorder fueling domestic far-right gains, which in turn worsens international cooperation) as the scenario most likely to produce a genuinely tragic outcome — relevant to European political-risk and populist-party tracking.
insights.quote: I think the most dangerous thing is if you get this kind of negative feedback loop between a much more dangerous and scary world, and then ethno-nationalist parties coming to power in great powers. And that could really take us into a much more tragic situation than where we are at the moment.

insights.claim: Kurt Campbell, drawing on his own experience as a student in Britain during the 1980s Pershing II missile deployment protests (when hundreds of thousands demonstrated weekly and a bestselling book titled 'The Disintegrating West' predicted the transatlantic relationship would never survive), argues that the alliance system has recovered from comparably severe crises of confidence before, once new U.S. leadership (in that case, Reagan) restored a sense of purpose.
insights.speaker: Kurt Campbell
insights.so_what: A first-hand historical parallel (1980s 'Disintegrating West' panic that proved wrong) offered as evidence that today's alliance pessimism may similarly overstate permanent damage — useful context for weighing how much credibility to give current 'alliances are dead' commentary against a base rate of prior false alarms.
insights.quote: I myself was a student in Great Britain during Reagan’s presidency when we were putting nuclear systems in Europe. I was a young guy but I had real questions about whether the special relationship would survive... I remember a book called The Disintegrating West, how it would never survive this period.
